content.comment_body: I have created a large home automation and alarm system project. It uses two [product_name] units with expanded input/output modules on a network, along with a [product_name] LTE module for remote access. My client refuses to pay for five months' work and has hired two individuals to change all admin passwords, gaining access to my proprietary software. Despite this, I can still connect remotely to these three controllers, but I cannot log in because the admin password has been altered. How is it possible that passwords were changed and my project copied? I apologize if this post is out of place, but I need advice on protecting my project from theft. Does [company_name] provide copyright protection or legal guidance? Please, if anyone can advise, let me know. Best regards, [user_name]
If you need direct assistance or information from [company_name], you should open a Support Request.

This issue is common—passwords can be hacked and ideas stolen. Unfortunately, that's typical nowadays. If you have a contract, you can pursue legal action. If you haven’t received payment after five months, was this a private project without a formal agreement? In that case, you can argue copyright ownership, but resolution will still require court proceedings. Regards, [user_name]

It's a complicated story. The client sued me and I'm currently under investigation because I stopped working for them and did not begin automating a new residence. To recover my payment, I'd have to continue working without any guarantee of being paid, so I refused and cancelled access and licenses for the controllers until payment is made. The client chose to involve hackers, changing administrator accounts for controllers and servers. We'll see how this unfolds... I remain the super administrator, but they continue to use my software and previously set administrator credentials after cracking my accounts. This situation involves privacy violations and intellectual property concerns.

We are now relying on recent European privacy legislation. The relevant information can be found here: [url]. We could seek damages—potentially up to tens of millions—because my software and Apple account are linked with a USA-based company [url]. The higher the value of the shared account, the greater the possible compensation, and the American legal system may be more effective in pursuing this. That's why I'm consulting [company_name] support, to reinforce my claim over project ownership and copyright. The client purchased all controllers and insists that software installed is entirely their property. I hope this clarifies my situation.
This is highly unusual business conduct from your client. I wish you good luck and hope the outcome is favorable. Regards, [user_name]

@[user_name], I hope you have a thorough contract; otherwise, you may be at a disadvantage and risk losing everything. Always draft a formal agreement for your work to present a professional image to your client. I'm concerned that in seeking reimbursement, you may incur more expenses. You can legally declare yourself the project designer, but in court you’ll need to prove your client commissioned the design. Regarding [product_name] controllers, the password protection is basic, similar to other entry-level models. Passwords are easy to retrieve with simple online research. Bear in mind the controller does not verify the password itself; that's handled by the software, and retrieval is straightforward. I'm not a hacker, but password discovery takes only seconds.

@[user_name], thank you for your response. [company_name] support reached out, but they're unable to assist further. As for my client, I had a contract for the WiFi and camera infrastructure, developed and invoiced the whole automation system monthly, and the client received these invoices. I believe I have a strong case in court. At this point I have nothing to lose—I've even recorded a video demonstrating server and controller login for legal evidence. If hacking the password is as easy as you imply, contact me privately; I'll share the IP address so you can attempt it yourself, change the password, and report back. If you need the original project file, let me know. The project for this residence can be seen on my website: [url]

Hi [user_name], I understand your frustration. I can't get involved due to potential legal complications. Even if you have proof, dealing with the Italian legal system could be slow. In the future, ensure all details are specified in a contract and use phased payments to minimize unpaid work. If you still have network access, consider researching online—there's information on password sniffing and hacking tools, including resources on Russian-language sites. I'm not a hacker myself, but I am both a developer and end user. I maintain strong relations with most suppliers and have complete password access for many systems (such as [version_no]), always respecting their rights and allowing them to benefit from updates or changes. A few times, when support was unavailable, I’ve had to retrieve passwords myself for maintenance, and I find this quicker than searching through all documented passwords. Note: I don't know who installed the controller (as shown in the photo), but the wiring quality is barely acceptable for testing and far from professional.

Hi, from my perspective, if you reconnect to a [product_name] controller without authorization it may violate the law. However, you mentioned your account is still in use—change it to prevent further unauthorized access. For upcoming projects, [product_name] offers a copy protection feature that prevents unauthorized duplication, using an MSD card. From my research, this appears secure so far. To enable it, insert the card into the controller, activate copy protection via the menu, copy your program to the card, erase the program from the controller unit, and reboot. Now, only the card can run the program; it can't be read or uploaded from the controller or the card, and removing the card disables the controller. If someone clones the card and uses it in another controller, it won't work. Be warned: you cannot modify the program afterward without the original [product_name] programming software file. You can set up a password alongside copy protection, but if the password is hacked, the program is still accessible. This is illegal, but if the customer is indifferent, there's little you can do. Hope this provides some help. Good luck.

analysis.insight_summary: Forum participants highlighted weak password security in [product_name] controllers, making them susceptible to unauthorized access and password changes. This compromises proprietary project files and administrative accounts, leading to intellectual property disputes where project owners retain some access but lose control over their work. While [company_name] provides only basic password protection, there is an advanced copy protection feature available using an MSD card. However, this requires deliberate implementation and is not commonly utilized.
analysis.user_expectations: The user anticipates [company_name] products to deliver robust security and reliable copyright protection to secure proprietary software. They seek legal and technical support to restore control and validate their project ownership. Enhanced access and program protection features are desired to prevent unauthorized copying and usage.
